title: Internet Security Glossary, Version 2
summary: A large glossary of information security terms, abbreviations, and explanations, meant to help authors of Internet documents use security vocabulary consistently. It gives recommendations on choosing terms: reuse the same term for the same concept, prefer plain dictionary meanings, and avoid terms that favor a particular vendor. It is informational and a handy reference.

eli5.summary: A giant dictionary of computer-safety words, so everyone who writes about internet security uses the same word for the same thing.

questions: what do security terms mean in rfcs

what do i d n o mean in rfc 4949

subtitle: A 334-page dictionary of security terms that tells RFC authors which words and definitions to use, and which to avoid.

tldr.problem: Internet documents use security words loosely, so the same word can mean different things in different RFCs, and different words can mean the same thing.
tldr.mechanism: The Glossary defines security terms, abbreviations and explanations, and marks every entry I, N, O or D to say whether authors should use it, use it with care, only mention it, or avoid it.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that replaces RFC 2828. Its recommendations are the author's opinions, not an official IETF position.

today: RFC 4949 is an Informational RFC (FYI 36) that obsoletes RFC 2828; the metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says its recommendations are the author's own opinions, not an IETF position.

sections.title: Why a Security Glossary
sections.content:
RFC 4949 is the Internet Security Glossary, Version 2. It gives definitions, abbreviations and explanations for information system security terms. Its purpose is to make material written in the Internet Standards Process easier to understand. The RFC calls such material IDOCs: RFCs, Internet-Drafts and other items of discourse.

The Abstract lists four principles for that writing: (a) use the same term or definition whenever the same concept is mentioned; (b) use terms in their plainest, dictionary sense; (c) use terms that are already well-established in open publications; and (d) avoid terms that favor a particular vendor, or a particular technology over competing ones.

The introduction ties these ideas to the goals of the Internet Standards Process: clear and concise documentation, technical excellence, prior implementation and testing, and openness and fairness. It even applies the robustness principle to prose: be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send. It also warns against "cute" synonyms such as "Green Book", which can confuse readers in another community.
sections.eli5: If every kid in a class used a different word for the same thing, nobody would understand the stories. The glossary is a shared word list so everyone means the same thing.

sections.title: Opinions, Not Standards
sections.content:
This Glossary is not an Internet Standard. A note from the RFC Editor at the top says the recommendations and particular interpretations in definitions are those of the author, not an official IETF position. The IETF took no formal position for or against them.

That includes the RFC 2119 words. When the Glossary says SHOULD NOT, it must be read as unofficial. The Glossary gives its reasons, especially for its SHOULD NOTs, so readers can decide for themselves whether to follow them.

The note adds a second caution: the Glossary is rich in the history of early network security work, but it may be somewhat incomplete in describing recent security work, which was developing rapidly. It also leans toward U.S. usage of English, and where it covers government and defense terminology it addresses only U.S. usage.
sections.eli5: It is like a coach's advice, not the official rulebook. The coach explains why, and you decide whether to follow it.

sections.title: How Each Entry Is Written
sections.content:
Entries are sorted in lexicographic order without regard to capitalization. Each one starts with a dollar sign and a space, so searching for $ X finds the defining entry for X and skips other entries that merely use the word. Proper nouns are capitalized and other entries are not. Every acronym used in the Glossary is defined in it, except items of common English such as "e.g." and "etc.".

Each entry carries a letter in parentheses for its definition type. A term with several meanings is numbered, with RECOMMENDED meanings listed first, and closely related meanings get letters such as 1a and 1b. A definition valid only in a certain context shows that context between slashes, for example /formal model/.

Many entries add labeled notes: Deprecated Abbreviation, Deprecated Definition, Deprecated Usage, Deprecated Term, Pronunciation, Derivation, Tutorial, Example and Usage. Cross-references appear as (See: X.) and (Compare: X). Explanatory text MAY be reused in IDOCs, but it does not override text in an IDOC that already uses the entry. The Glossary also adopts the "new" or logical punctuation style of programmers, where quotation marks act as balanced delimiters, and recommends it for IDOCs.
sections.eli5: Every word in the dictionary has a little tag and sometimes a note, such as a story that explains it or a warning to skip it. A dollar sign marks where each new word starts so you can find it fast.

sections.title: The Four Entry Types: I, N, O and D
sections.content:
The letter on each entry says whether an author should use that term and definition.

  • I: RECOMMENDED, of Internet origin, or generic enough that the Glossary can define it freely. Some carry a Usage note that limits the context.
  • N: RECOMMENDED if needed at all, but of non-Internet origin. Authors should not use the term outside its stated context or limit.
  • O: not recommended, but worth knowing. It SHOULD NOT be used in IDOCs unless the term is clearly identified as non-Internet.
  • D: deprecated. It SHOULD NOT be used, and a note explains why.

Sometimes an official definition from a government, industry or standards body is suitable, and the Glossary marks it N. When one is too narrow or outdated, the Glossary marks it O and puts an I or N entry before it that is meant to supersede it. For "security service", the O definition covers only communication services provided by layers of the OSI reference model, while the new I definition fits more situations.
sections.eli5: It is like traffic lights for words. Green means use it, yellow means use it carefully, blue means just know it exists, and red means please do not use it.

sections.title: Threats, Vulnerabilities, Attacks and Risk
sections.content:
Section 4 holds the definitions. The entries show the method well, because they separate ideas that people often mix up. A vulnerability is a flaw or weakness in a system's design, implementation, or operation and management that could be exploited to violate its security policy. A threat is a potential for violation of security, which exists when there is an entity, circumstance, capability, action, or event that could cause harm. An attack is an intentional act by which an entity attempts to evade security services and violate the security policy.

The threat entry notes that "threat" is frequently misused to mean either "threat action" or "vulnerability". It deprecates one definition, "an indication of an impending undesirable event", because that wording is ambiguous. A threat action is the realization of a threat, and a threat consequence is the security violation that results. The four basic consequences are unauthorized disclosure, deception, disruption and usurpation.

Risk is an expectation of loss, expressed as the probability that a particular threat will exploit a particular vulnerability with a particular harmful result. The tutorial lists four ways to deal with it: risk avoidance, risk transference, risk limitation and risk assumption. Quoting "Courtney's laws", the Glossary also notes that perfect security has infinite cost and that there is no such thing as zero risk.
sections.eli5: A vulnerability is an unlocked window. A threat is a burglar who might come. An attack is the burglar trying the window. Risk is how likely it is, and how bad, if they get in.

sections.title: Samples: Authentication, Signatures and PKI
sections.content:
Many entries pair a definition with a short tutorial. Authentication is the process of verifying a claim that a system entity or resource has a certain attribute value. The tutorial says it has two steps: an identification step, presenting the claimed attribute such as a user identifier, and a verification step, presenting evidence that binds the attribute to what it is claimed for.

A digital signature is a value computed with a cryptographic algorithm and associated with a data object so that any recipient can verify the data's origin and integrity. The data is first hashed, then the hash result is transformed with the signer's private key. A public-key infrastructure (PKI) is a system of certification authorities, and optionally registration authorities and other supporting servers and agents, that handle certificate, key, archive and token management for a community of users. Its core functions are to register users and issue public-key certificates, to revoke certificates when required, and to archive data needed to validate certificates later.

Other entries cover named systems. Kerberos, for example, is described as a system developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology that uses passwords and symmetric cryptography to provide ticket-based peer entity authentication and access control in a client-server network, with the Kerberos specification given as RFC 4120. The man-in-the-middle attack entry shows how Diffie-Hellman-Merkle key exchange without data origin authentication lets an attacker pose as each party to the other. Entries like these point the reader to the RFCs and outside standards that define the details.
sections.eli5: Showing your library card proves who you are. A signature on a letter proves who wrote it and that nobody changed it. A PKI is the office that hands out and cancels the cards.

sections.title: Sources, References and the Earlier Glossary
sections.content:
The RFC Editor Note calls this document both a major revision and a major expansion of the Security Glossary in RFC 2828, which it obsoletes. Section 1 also points to other glossaries of general networking terms, such as RFC 1208 and RFC 1983, and includes only a few non-security networking terms to stay self-contained.

Section 7 is a long list of informative references. Because the Glossary focuses on the Internet Standards Process, the list emphasizes international, governmental and industrial standards documents. Some RFCs especially relevant to security are cited in entries in square brackets (for example [R1457] under "security label") and are listed there. Others are mentioned in parentheses, for example RFC 959 under "File Transport Protocol", and are not listed. The only normative reference is RFC 2119 for the key words.
sections.eli5: This dictionary is the newer, bigger edition of an older one. At the back it lists the books and papers where its facts came from.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's own Security Considerations section is brief. The document mainly defines security terms and recommends how to use them. It also offers limited tutorial information about security aspects of Internet protocols. It does not describe in detail the vulnerabilities of, or threats to, specific protocols, and it does not definitively describe the mechanisms that protect specific protocols.

In practice this means the Glossary is a vocabulary aid. Readers who need the real security analysis of a protocol should turn to that protocol's own specification, such as the ones the entries cite.
sections.eli5: The dictionary tells you what words mean. It does not tell you how to lock up every particular computer system. For that, read that system's own instructions.

viz.caption: THE FOUR DEFINITION TYPES IN RFC 4949

items.label: Recommended, Internet origin
items.desc: Authors are encouraged to use this term and definition.

items.label: Recommended, non-Internet origin
items.desc: Use only within the stated context or limit, if needed at all.

items.label: Other, to be noted
items.desc: Not for IDOCs unless identified as non-Internet.

items.label: Deprecated
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be used in Internet documents.

items.title: Unauthorized disclosure
items.text: An entity gains access to information it is not authorized to have.

items.title: Deception
items.text: An authorized entity receives false data and believes it to be true.

items.title: Disruption
items.text: System services or functions are interrupted or prevented from operating correctly.

items.title: Usurpation
items.text: An unauthorized entity gains control of system services or functions.

viz.caption: FOUR WAYS TO DEAL WITH A RISK

cells: Eliminate the risk by countering the threat or removing the vulnerability.
Shift the risk to another system or entity, such as buying insurance.
Limit the risk with controls that minimize the resulting loss.
Accept the potential for loss and continue operating the system.
